title: Verifier‑Assisted versus LLM‑Only Pre‑deployment Network‑Change Validation: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We measured whether integrating a deterministic pre‑deployment verifier with a bounded automated repair budget increases the fraction of intent‑driven network‑change proposals that pass semantic validation compared with accepting a single LLM candidate. In a preregistered paired design (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) we executed 300 paired intents (100 per difficulty stratum: low/medium/high) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic semantic validator. Each paired intent produced one shared_initial generation that was evaluated under two conditions: baseline (accept single shot) and guarded (deterministic validation and ≤1 automated repair). Outcomes: baseline 299/300 unflagged passes (0.996667), guarded 300/300 (1.0); contingency n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00,0.01] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, B = 10000). Under the supplied synthetic suite and repair budget the single‑shot generator was near ceiling, limiting observable deterministic rescue. We archive preregistration, execution, and analysis artifacts and interpret results with respect to estimand conditioning, validator coverage, repair budget, and operational deployment policies.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, template synthesis, and automated repair. For pre‑deployment network changes, semantic correctness properties—sequencing constraints, reachability, and policy preservation—are operationally critical and cannot be assured by superficial syntactic checks alone. A common engineering pattern is to pair generative models with deterministic validators and bounded automated repair (generate→validate→repair) to reduce operational risk. Yet the measurable benefit of such guarded pipelines depends on what is held fixed (the estimand), the single‑shot quality of the generator, the validator's expressiveness, and the allowed repair budget.

We preregistered and executed a paired experiment (study id cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) that isolates the deterministic rescue obtainable when the same single LLM candidate is evaluated under two treatments. For each intent the pipeline produced exactly one shared_initial candidate and compared: (a) baseline — accept the single candidate without repair, and (b) guarded — run a deterministic validator and allow at most one automated repair which itself is re‑validated. Our primary research question: does adding a deterministic verifier plus at most one automated repair increase the probability that a single LLM candidate passes semantic pre‑deployment validation compared with accepting that same candidate without repair?

Contributions: (1) a preregistered paired evaluation isolating deterministic rescue under a shared_initial estimand; (2) complete archived execution and analysis artifacts supporting deterministic replay; and (3) an evidence‑grounded interpretation of ceiling effects, estimand conditioning, validator coverage, and operational implications for NetOps CI/CD policies.
sections.related_work:
Recent surveys and system reports document active application of LLMs to NetOps tasks including intent translation, configuration synthesis, and automated repair [1–4]. Several system papers emphasize tool augmentation and planner‑centric frameworks that enable LLMs to call external validators, simulators, or synthesizers to coordinate multi‑step NetOps workflows [2,5]. Empirical reports show that introducing deterministic checks and generate→validate→repair scaffolds can improve correctness metrics relative to unconstrained generation, but effect size depends strongly on validator coverage, task distribution, and whether pipelines permit resampling or verifier‑guided regeneration [3,4].

Methodological work highlights that many prior evaluations conflate benefits from deterministic validation with benefits from multiple independent model draws or interactive regeneration; this conflation obscures the bounded, post‑hoc rescue attributable purely to a validator plus constrained repair [5,6]. Other literature on hallucination detection and safety nets proposes entropy‑ and semantic‑consistency detectors and retrieval augmentation to reduce false positives in high‑stakes domains; their NetOps applicability depends on threat model and validator semantics [7]. Finally, hybrid repair approaches that combine symbolic fault localization with generative repair operators report variable success across fault classes, underscoring the role of verifier expressiveness and the allowed repair operator set [8].

Our study sits within these threads but differs by (a) conditioning on a single LLM draw per intent (the shared_initial estimand) to isolate deterministic validator/repair rescue, and (b) fixing a tightly bounded repair budget (≤1 edit) to quantify low‑cost deterministic rescue under operational model‑call constraints.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The study was preregistered (cnsmp2026-llm-verifier-predeployment-001) prior to the confirmatory run. The primary estimand is the absolute paired difference in the unflagged verifier‑pass proportion (guarded − baseline) computed on N = 300 paired intents after applying preregistered inclusion/exclusion rules. The preregistration specified a paired design, a single confirmatory hypothesis, exact McNemar two‑sided testing, and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (seed = 1729, B = 10,000). The preregistration SHA‑256 is archived with the run.

Task suite and stratification. Tasks were generated deterministically by the registered task generator into a synthetic_topology_suite stratified into three difficulty levels (low/medium/high). Each task encodes the natural‑language intent, initial and expected final device states, sequencing constraints (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields), preserve_unspecified_state invariants, and protected_interfaces. The confirmatory run sampled 100 pairs per stratum for a total of 300 paired intents.

Shared_initial protocol, models, validator, and repair operator. To isolate deterministic rescue from resampling effects, the shared_initial protocol produced exactly one LLM candidate per pair that was reused for both baseline and guarded conditions. Generation used the declared model gpt-5-mini (execution configuration declares requested_model = "gpt-5-mini"). Semantic evaluation employed a deterministic validator implementing full intent‑constraint checks (sequencing, required command counts, preservation of unspecified state, and topology‑encoded reachability invariants). The guarded pipeline permitted at most one automated repair attempt per pair; the repair operator is a constrained edit routine limited to localized sequencing and insertion edits (for example, inserting a missing 'admin down' before a VLAN/MTU change). Repair attempts were applied only when the validator flagged the shared_initial candidate and were themselves deterministically re‑validated.

Execution, stopping rules, and contamination controls. The run executed under a scientific_confirmatory adapter enforcing the preregistered stopping rule and model‑call budget. Pairs were excluded only if both pipeline calls failed due to provider/infrastructure outage; no such exclusions occurred. The preregistration included negative controls and deterministic contamination checks (reachability invariants and forbidden‑template protections); automated flagging rules treated unexpected negative‑control passes as contamination.

Analysis plan. The preregistered confirmatory analysis used a paired binary executor to produce contingency counts (n11,n10,n01,n00), the absolute paired difference, an exact two‑sided McNemar test, and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (seed = 1729, B = 10,000). Secondary stratum tests and sensitivity analyses were designated exploratory and subject to multiplicity control where reported.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The adapter completed planned work yielding 600 episodes (300 pairs) under the shared_initial protocol. Model calls used = 301 (300 shared_initial generations plus one repair invocation), and the repair stage_count observed = 1. No provider/infrastructure outages or pair exclusions occurred.

Primary outcomes. Binary scoring produced baseline_success_count = 299 and guarded_success_count = 300, i.e., baseline = 299/300 (0.9966667) and guarded = 300/300 (1.0). The paired contingency counts are n11 = 299, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The absolute paired improvement (guarded − baseline) = 0.0033333. Exact two‑sided McNemar test (based on discordant counts n10 and n01) returned p = 1.0. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval (seed = 1729, B = 10000) is [0.00, 0.01]. The minimal discordance (m = n10 + n01 = 1) limits inferential sensitivity: the exact test has no power to detect small differences when baseline performance is near ceiling.

Per‑stratum diagnostics and repair trace. Per‑stratum tallies were: low baseline = 100/100 and guarded = 100/100; medium baseline = 100/100 and guarded = 100/100; high baseline = 99/100 and guarded = 100/100. The single discordant pair (high stratum) invoked the permitted automated repair. Validator traces attribute the initial failure to a sequencing omission (a required 'admin down' step missing before a VLAN/MTU change). The constrained repair performed a single localized insertion of the missing sequencing command, after which the validator reported a pass. That repair produced the only deterministic rescue observed; the repair transcript and before/after validator traces are archived with the run bundle.

Contamination and missingness. Contamination checks signaled no anomalies; missingness summary shows zero failed or unscorable episodes and no excluded pairs. These summaries are archived with the analysis artifacts.

Operational cost. The guarded pipeline incurred a single additional repair stage call across 300 pairs (model_calls_used = 301), indicating minimal extra model‑call cost for the observed deterministic rescue under the chosen repair operator and budget.
sections.discussion:
Estimand conditioning and operational meaning. Conditioning on a single LLM draw per intent (shared_initial) corresponds to operational policies that tightly constrain model calls for cost, latency, or governance reasons. Under such policies the guarded pipeline measures only deterministic validator and bounded repair rescue applied to the identical candidate. Pipelines that permit resampling or verifier‑guided regeneration change the estimand and typically increase achievable success rates by exploiting generator variance; such workflows require separate preregistered evaluation.

Ceiling effects and the missing pilot. The preregistration planned an optional pilot (n = 60) to estimate discordance for power calibration; that pilot was not executed. As a result the main run encountered a near‑ceiling baseline (299/300), producing minimal discordance (m = 1) and reduced power to detect small absolute improvements. This practical outcome underscores the value of small calibration pilots when generator performance may approach ceiling on chosen task suites.

Validator coverage and failure‑mode dependence. The single observed failure mode was a sequencing omission; other classes (reachability violations, forbidden ACL removal) did not appear at scale in this synthetic suite. The marginal utility of a guarded pipeline therefore depends on (a) the deployment distribution of failure modes and (b) validator expressiveness. Richer validators that check reachability or complex ACL semantics could increase observed rescue rates; conversely, operator policies that forbid automated edits reduce the guarded pipeline to a detection and escalation mechanism.

Repair budget tradeoffs. We intentionally limited automated repair to a single constrained edit to measure bounded deterministic rescue. Iterative repair, larger edit operators, or interactive verifier‑guided generation would likely increase rescue opportunities but represent different operational tradeoffs (higher model‑call cost, increased automation risk) and require a different estimand and preregistered design.

Implications for NetOps CI/CD. Organizations should align evaluation estimands with operational constraints: if model‑call budgets are tight, the shared_initial estimand provides a meaningful lower bound on achievable deterministic rescue via validator+bounded repair. If pipelines permit resampling or interactive steering, evaluations must reflect those policies to estimate practical success rates. Our archived execution accounting shows that bounded deterministic repair can produce low‑cost rescues in some cases, but the absolute gain depends on baseline generator quality and the validator's semantic scope.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired comparison between a verifier‑assisted pipeline (deterministic validator + ≤1 automated repair) and accepting a single‑shot LLM candidate under the shared_initial estimand on 300 synthetic NetOps intents using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic semantic validator. Baseline single‑shot generation produced 299/300 unflagged verifier passes and the guarded pipeline 300/300, yielding an absolute paired improvement of 0.00333 (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.01]). Deterministic validator+repair rescued one sequencing omission under the bounded repair budget. The near‑ceiling baseline limits inferential sensitivity to small absolute improvements under the shared_initial estimand. We release full preregistration, execution, and analysis artifacts so follow‑up studies can vary estimand conditioning, model strength, task distribution, or repair budget to quantify tradeoffs relevant to operational NetOps CI/CD policies.

limitations: Synthetic benchmark: tasks and topologies were produced by a deterministic generator; real‑world heterogeneity may expose different failure modes and increase verifier marginal utility.
Single model and validator: only gpt-5-mini and the evaluated deterministic validator were used; results may not generalize to other LLMs or richer/diverse validators.

Ceiling effect: baseline single‑shot performance was near 100% on this suite (299/300), producing limited discordance and reduced power to detect small absolute improvements relative to larger pre‑specified targets.
Pilot not executed: the preregistered pilot intended for discordance estimation and power calibration was not run; no post‑preregistration power recalculation was performed.

Estimand conditioning: the shared_initial protocol conditions the estimand on a single LLM candidate and therefore does not measure verifier benefit that would arise from allowing independent alternative LLM candidates per condition (resampling or iterative generation).
Repair budget: the guarded condition permitted at most one automated repair per pair; larger or iterative repair strategies may yield different outcomes.
